question.text: A wire of length <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>L</mi></math> and radius <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>r</mi></math> is clamped rigidly at one end. When the other end of the wire is pulled by a force <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>F</mi></math>, its length increases by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>5</mn><mo> </mo><mi>cm</mi></math>. Another wire of the same material of length <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>4</mn><mo> </mo><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi></math> and radius <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>4</mn><mi>r</mi></math> is pulled by a force <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>4</mn><mo> </mo><mi>F</mi></math> under same conditions. The increase in length of this wire is _____ <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>cm</mi></math>.

solution.text:
Young's modulus is given by Y=FLA∆L, here, A is cross-section area and ∆L is change in length.

Now, when force F is applied, change in length ΔL1=FLAY=FLπr2Y=5 cm

Now, when force 4F is applied, change in length

ΔL2=4 F4Lπ16r2Y=FLπr2Y=5 cm
